topics: 🕯️ Fire That Rested — Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: rested from labor of transgression; a lantern that burned all Shabbat
🔥 A Gentile's Flame — Jew from gentile is fine, gentile from gentile is decreed; is a flame one entity?
🏙️ Fire Seen Outside the City — majorities, a child with a torch, furnaces, ovens, and synagogue lights
🌿 Spices Not Meant for Fragrance — the dead, the bathroom, the perfumer's shop, Tiberias and Tzippori
👀 'Until One Benefits From Its Light' — Rav vs. Rava, coins and weights, and not chasing after fire
💰 Returning to Bless — willful vs. forgetful, the purse on the Temple Mount, a lion, and a golden dove
🙏 Amen and Oil — 'seize and bless', schoolchildren, and 'you shall sanctify yourselves' at the meal's end

overview.title: 📖 Overview: The Havdala Flame and Ending the Chapter
overview.subtitle: Berakhot 53a–53b
overview.hebrewSource: אֵין מְחַזְּרִין עַל הָאוּר כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁמְחַזְּרִים עַל הַמִּצְוֹת
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf is almost entirely about the havdala blessing over fire and spices. Which flame counts as having 'rested' on Shabbat, whose candle may be used, what to do with a fire glimpsed outside a city, and which fires exist for light rather than heat or honor. Spices follow the same logic: no blessing unless they are meant for fragrance. The mishna's 'until one benefits from its light' splits Rav from Rava. The Gemara then returns to the mishna's last cases — one who forgot Grace after Meals, how long digestion lasts, answering amen — and closes the chapter with oil for the hands and the verse 'you shall sanctify yourselves'.

slides.title: 🕯️ Which Flame 'Rested' on Shabbat?
slides.subtitle: Defining the baraita's term, then the puzzle of a flame passed from one candle to another

nodes.content: ❓ 'Fire that rested' — rested from all labor, even permitted labor? But a baraita blesses over fire lit on Shabbat for a woman in childbirth or a dangerously ill person!
✅ Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: 'rested' means rested from labor of transgression. A lantern that burned the whole of Shabbat may be blessed at its conclusion.
📜 Baraita: a gentile who lit from a Jew, or a Jew who lit from a gentile — bless. A gentile who lit from a gentile — do not bless.

❓ If the problem is a flame that did not rest, a Jew lighting from a gentile also did not rest! Is the new flame a different entity? No — one who carries a flame into the public domain on Shabbat is liable, so the flame is one entity.

columns.label: Jew from gentile
columns.content: The forbidden flame is still there, but one blesses over the permitted addition that came into being in the Jew's hand.

columns.label: Gentile from gentile
columns.content: By right the same should apply — but the Sages decreed because of the first gentile and the first pillar of flame kindled on Shabbat.

slides.title: 🏙️ Fire Seen From Outside the City
slides.subtitle: A string of baraitot on when a passer-by may use a flame for havdala
rows: City with a majority of gentiles
Majority Jews, or half and half
The baraita should have said 'even half'; it said 'majority Jews' only to match the first clause
Check — bless if the child is Jewish
Rav: it is right after sunset; an adult with fire is surely a gentile, but a child may be a Jew who just picked it up
A fire at least as thick as a furnace opening
A fire that size is kindled for light too
Fire of a furnace, oven, or stove
One baraita: bless; another: do not
At the start it is only for heating; at the end its light is used
Light of a synagogue or study hall
One baraita: bless; another: do not
Depends whether an important person is present (lit for honor), whether there is a caretaker who uses it, or whether there is moonlight

callout.label: One blessing or many?
callout.text: Fire brought into the study hall: Beit Shammai — each person blesses for himself, to avoid interrupting study (the house of Rabban Gamliel would not even say 'good health' after a sneeze there). Beit Hillel — one blesses for all, for 'the splendor of the King is in the multitude of the people' (Proverbs 14:28).

slides.title: 🌿 Spices: Only If Meant for Fragrance
slides.subtitle: The mishna bans the candle and spices of the dead; the Gemara extends the principle

boxes.title: No blessing
items: Candle of the dead — lit for honor, not light (Rav: if it is carried out by day and night it is for honor; only at night, it is for light and one may bless)
Spices of the dead — to remove the odor
Rav Huna: bathroom spices and oil that removes filth
Rabbi Yoḥanan: incense smelled in Tiberias on Shabbat eve or Tzippori after Shabbat — presumed for perfuming garments
Rabbi Yosei: even a majority-Jewish town, since some burn incense for witchcraft and some for garments — the majority is not for fragrance

boxes.title: Blessing
items: Baraita: a scent outside a town with a Jewish majority
The perfumer's shop — the scent is for fragrance, so customers will come and buy
Sitting there all day: bless once; entering and leaving repeatedly: bless each time

boxes.title: Forbidden to smell
items: One walking through an idolaters' market who wants to smell the incense is a sinner

slides.title: 👀 'Until They Benefit From Its Light' — Literally or Potentially?
slides.subtitle: Rav and Rava read the mishna differently, and the amora'im act accordingly

lines.speaker: Rav
lines.text: Not literal benefit: if standing close he could use its light, he may bless even from a distance. Rav Ashi agrees: 'from a distance' is what we learned.

lines.speaker: Objection
lines.text: Tosefta: a candle hidden in one's lap or in a lantern, or seeing a flame without using its light, or using its light without seeing the flame — no blessing until he both sees the flame and uses its light. 'Sees but does not use' — isn't that distance?

lines.speaker: Rav's side
lines.text: No, it is a flame that is gradually dimming (עוֹמְמוֹת, spelled with an ayin, from 'the cedars could not dim it', Ezekiel 31:8). Rav Ḥisda: coals are 'glowing' if a chip placed among them ignites by itself.

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: 'Benefit' is literal. How close? Ulla: enough to tell an issar from a pundeyon. Ḥizkiya: to tell a Tiberian weight from a Tzippori weight.

lines.speaker: Practice
lines.text: Rav Yehuda blessed on the light of Adda the servant's house, far away; Rava on Gurya bar Ḥama's house, next door; Abaye on the house of bar Avuh.

lines.speaker: Rav
lines.text: One does not seek out fire the way one seeks out other mitzvot. Rabbi Zeira: I used to search; once I heard this, I bless only if a flame comes my way.

slides.title: 💰 Forgot Grace: Go Back, or Bless Where You Are?
slides.subtitle: The Houses argue by parable, and the Gemara tells two stories that settle the mood

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rav Zevid (or Rav Dimi bar Abba): the dispute is only about one who forgot; if he skipped the blessing deliberately, all agree he must return — the mishna's word 'forgot' is precise

2️⃣ Beit Hillel: by your view, one who ate atop the Temple Mount and came down must climb back up? Beit Shammai: if he forgot his purse up there he would climb for his own honor — all the more so for the honor of Heaven!
3️⃣ Two students: one forgot, went back like Beit Shammai, and found a purse of gold; one acted deliberately, did not return, and was eaten by a lion

4️⃣ Rabba bar bar Ḥana, traveling with a caravan, told them 'I forgot a golden dove' so they would wait; he went back, blessed, and found a golden dove — Israel is likened to a dove (Psalms 68:14), saved only by its wings, i.e. by mitzvot

callout.label: Closing the chapter:
callout.text: Digestion: Rabbi Yoḥanan — as long as he is not hungry; Reish Lakish — as long as he is thirsty from eating, or four mil after a large meal. Amen: Rav told his son 'seize the chance and bless', yet Rabbi Yosei says the one who answers amen is greater (Rabbi Nehorai: the mighty who finish the battle) — a tannaitic dispute. No amen after schoolchildren practicing. Oil for the hands: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak knows only the baraita on 'you shall sanctify yourselves' (Leviticus 20:26) — first waters, final waters, oil, and the blessing.

summary.principle: A havdala blessing over fire or spices requires a flame that rested from forbidden labor and is meant for light, and spices meant for fragrance — and one need not chase after fire the way one pursues other mitzvot.

flowSteps.content: 🕯️ 'Rested' = rested from labor of transgression; a Jew lighting from a gentile blesses on the permitted addition; gentile from gentile is a decree
🏙️ Fire outside a city: majority Jews (even half) yes; child with torch — check; furnace, oven, synagogue — only when the light is actually used
🌿 Spices: no blessing for the dead, the bathroom, garment-perfuming, or witchcraft; yes for the perfumer's shop

columns.content: 👀 Rav: potential benefit suffices; Rava: actual benefit — enough to tell an issar from a pundeyon
💰 Forgot Grace: deliberate — all return; a purse of gold vs. a lion; Rabba bar bar Ḥana's golden dove

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: 'You shall sanctify yourselves' — first waters; 'you shall be holy' — final waters; 'for holy' — oil; 'I am the Lord your God' — the blessing

quiz.q: According to Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak, what does 'fire that rested' mean?
o: Fire that was not burning at all on Shabbat
Fire that rested from any labor, even permitted labor
Fire that rested from labor of transgression, even if it burned all Shabbat
Fire lit by a Jew after Shabbat ended
quiz.e: A flame lit permissibly (for the ill) or burning throughout Shabbat may be blessed; only fire produced through forbidden labor is excluded.

quiz.q: Why may one bless over a flame that a Jew lit from a gentile's candle, but not over one a gentile lit from a gentile?
o: Because a flame is a new entity every moment, so a Jew's flame is fresh
Because one blesses on the permitted addition to the flame, but the Sages decreed against gentile-from-gentile because of the first gentile and first pillar of flame
Because a gentile's candle never rests
Because only a Jew's candle contains many lights
quiz.e: The Gemara rejects the 'new entity' idea from the law of carrying a flame on Shabbat, then explains that one blesses on the permitted addition; gentile-from-gentile is fundamentally the same but was banned by decree.

quiz.q: Why does the baraita specify a child holding a torch outside the city, rather than an adult?
o: Children are presumed to be Jewish
Right after sunset an adult with fire is surely a gentile, whereas a child may be a Jew who happened to take it
A child's torch is always thick as a furnace opening
An adult's torch is lit for honor
quiz.e: Rav explains that the case is shortly after sunset: a Jewish adult would not rush to take fire immediately after Shabbat, so only a child leaves room for doubt.

quiz.q: What is the difference between Rav and Rava regarding 'one does not bless over the candle until they benefit from its light'?
o: Rav requires actual benefit; Rava says potential benefit suffices
Rav says potential benefit (if he stood close) suffices; Rava requires actual benefit, enough to distinguish an issar from a pundeyon
Rav permits blessing over coals; Rava forbids it
Rav forbids blessing at a distance; Rava permits it
quiz.e: Rav reads 'benefit' non-literally and permits blessing from afar; Rava reads it literally, and Ulla and Ḥizkiya give measures of nearness.

quiz.q: What did Rabba bar bar Ḥana tell his caravan so they would wait while he returned to recite Grace after Meals?
o: That he had forgotten to recite a blessing
That he had forgotten a purse of gold
That he had forgotten a golden dove
That a lion was following them
quiz.e: He feared they would tell him to bless where he stood, so he said he forgot a golden dove; he went back, blessed, and found one — a dove symbolizing Israel, saved by its wings as Israel is by mitzvot.
